_mock_note: Section 8 output, generated by agents/explanation.py from plan_bundle.json - this is no longer hand-written prose. Regenerate it whenever a plan number changes. The numbers themselves are still stated by hand in plan_bundle.json, which is what keeps tests/test_pipeline.py meaningful: if this file were the only statement of the expected output, the test would be comparing the code against itself. Two things to notice. The prose deliberately does not say 'twenty years of returns', because no field states the dataset length - provenance like that belongs in meta and on the trust panel, not in agent prose. And numbers written as words ('five years', 'two occasions') are still declared in numbers_used, because a digit-only regex will not catch them.

plans_text.headline: Invest 35,000 a month, weighted towards debt
plans_text.body: This plan puts 40% of your monthly investment into equity and 60% into debt, and reaches a projected 26,60,000 against your 25,00,000 target in five years. It asks for 35,000 of your 45,000 monthly surplus, which leaves you 10,000 of breathing room each month. Out of 10,000 simulations run on real historical market returns, 8,700 reached your goal. It also held up against every combination of shock events we tested.

plans_text.headline: Invest 52,000 a month, mostly in equity
plans_text.body: This plan puts 85% of your monthly investment into equity and 15% into debt, and reaches a projected 44,10,000 against your 25,00,000 target in five years. It is not affordable on your current finances: it needs 52,000 a month against a surplus of 45,000, leaving you 7,000 short every month. Out of 10,000 simulations run on real historical market returns, 9,500 reached your goal. It does not survive our stress test: "Appraisal comes in at 4% instead of 10%", "Family medical expense" and "Landlord raises rent by 15%" landing together would leave you 6,90,000 short of the goal.

goal_priority_note: Your house downpayment is funded first because it is five years away, while the child education goal is twelve years out and can absorb a slower start. The nearer deadline is the binding one, so it sets the monthly figure.
mismatch_note: You described your approach as aggressive, but your transaction history looks moderate. On two occasions you sold equity within days of a market fall. That matters here because the plans with the highest projected returns are exactly the ones that fall furthest during a bad year, and a plan left early performs worse than a slower plan held to the end.
